q: A person has fallen down with sudden loss of consciousness. On examinations his vitals are stable with right eyeball deviated upwards. Pupils are contracting on projection of light. Where of the following structures likely damaged?
e:
Right eye deviated UPWARDS = right superior oblique is not working (it normally pulls an adducted eye down), so inferior oblique/superior rectus act unopposed. Pupils constrict to light = III nerve and Edinger-Westphal pathway intact. So only the IV nerve pathway is affected. The trochlear nucleus lies in the dorsal midbrain and its fibres cross (decussate) before supplying the CONTRALATERAL superior oblique. Right eye weakness therefore means a LEFT IV nucleus lesion.
Key points
IV is the only cranial nerve that exits dorsally and crosses.
Nuclear lesion = contralateral eye.
peripheral nerve lesion = ipsilateral eye.
Patients tilt the head away from the paretic eye to avoid diplopia.
Why not the other options
Right IV nucleus would affect the LEFT eye. VI nucleus lesions (pons) paralyse lateral rectus, so the eye turns inward (convergent squint), never upward.

q: A 75-year-old male who is a known diabetic and hypertensive but irregular on medication, suddenly fallen down unconsciously. He was rushed to emergency physician. On examination after regaining consciousness, he is unable to close the right eye & no wrinkles are formed on right forehead. His right angle of mouth is deviated downward. Which of the following lesion is correct?
e:
Cannot close the right eye + no wrinkles on the right forehead + right mouth angle drooping = the WHOLE right half of the face (upper and lower) is paralysed. A lower motor neuron (facial nucleus/nerve) lesion paralyses every muscle it supplies on the same side, including frontalis and orbicularis oculi: right facial LMN lesion.
Key points
Bell's palsy = LMN (forehead involved)
Stroke = UMN (forehead spared)
Diabetes and hypertension are risk factors for LMN palsy too.
| Page : 1
Why not the other options
UMN (corticobulbar) lesions spare the forehead because the upper face receives bilateral cortical input; only the contralateral lower face is weak. So right/left UMN is wrong, and a left LMN lesion would paralyse the left side.

q: A 40-year-old female has come to surgical OPD with swelling in the midline of the neck. Surgeon examined the mass and confirmed as thyroid gland enlargement. Pathological examination showed the swelling as medullary carcinoma of thyroid. Surgeon after doing total thyroidectomy post operative day 1 the patient developed breathlessness and hoarseness of voice. Which of the following nerves are damaged during surgery?
e:
Medullary carcinoma needing total thyroidectomy; on post-op day 1 breathlessness (airway narrowing) and hoarseness (vocal cord dysfunction). These point to injury of the nerve supplying the vocal cord muscles. The recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies all intrinsic laryngeal muscles except cricothyroid, including the abductor (posterior cricoarytenoid). It runs in the tracheo-oesophageal groove close to the inferior thyroid artery, so it is easily injured.
Key points
Bilateral RLN palsy causes stridor and may need tracheostomy.
Remember: the RLN lies close to the inferior thyroid artery and the external laryngeal nerve to the superior thyroid artery.
Why not the other options
External laryngeal nerve supplies only cricothyroid, causing a weak, monotone voice without breathlessness. Internal laryngeal nerve is sensory above the cords (aspiration, cough). Jacobson's nerve is the tympanic branch of IX (middle ear).

q: A 60-year-old diabetic patient has the complaints of pain in the throat. On examination of his throat his uvula is deviated to right side. Also gag reflex is lost. Which of the following is likely damaged?
e:
Uvula deviated to the right + loss of gag reflex + diabetic with throat pain = palatal muscle paralysis on one side (IX/X pathway). The uvula is pulled towards the healthy side, so the weak side is the LEFT. Palatal muscles (levator veli palatini, musculus uvulae) are supplied by the cranial root of the accessory nerve through the vagus (pharyngeal plexus). Left cranial accessory nerve lesion.
Key points
Gag reflex = afferent glossopharyngeal (IX), efferent vagus (X)
In vagal palsy the uvula deviates AWAY from the lesion.
Why not the other options
Right-sided lesions would pull the uvula to the left. The spinal accessory nerve supplies only sternocleidomastoid and trapezius, not the palate.
| Page : 2

q: Which of the following is the feature of the Brown Sequard syndrome?
e:
The question asks for a feature of Brown-Sequard syndrome (functional hemisection of the spinal cord). The dorsal columns (fine touch, vibration, proprioception) ascend UNCROSSED, so below the lesion they are lost on the SAME side. The corticospinal tract (crossed in the medulla) gives ipsilateral UMN paralysis.
Key points
Ipsilateral: paralysis + dorsal column loss.
contralateral: pain and temperature loss.
Why not the other options
Pain, temperature and crude touch travel in the spinothalamic tract which crosses within 1-2 segments, so they are lost on the OPPOSITE side. Hence 'ipsilateral loss of pain/crude touch' and 'contralateral paralysis' are wrong.

q: A person came to emergency department with periorbital swelling & proptosis. Also, difficulty in the movement of eyeball in the right side. Referred pain in present in tip of nose and upper eyelid. Also, a history of laceration injury in the scalp is observed. Which of the following layers got damaged in scalp?
e:
Periorbital swelling, proptosis, restricted eye movement and referred pain to the nose tip/upper eyelid (V1) = cavernous sinus involvement after a scalp laceration. The 4th scalp layer (loose areolar tissue, the 'danger area') contains emissary veins that connect to the diploic veins and the dural venous sinuses, so infection spreads inwards to the cavernous sinus.
Key points
SCALP = Skin, Connective tissue, Aponeurosis (galea), Loose areolar tissue, Pericranium.
Why not the other options
Skin and dense connective tissue (1st and 2nd layers) and the aponeurosis (3rd) are firmly bound; periosteum (5th) is attached to bone and does not allow spread like the loose layer.

q: Which of the following is not true for the bronchopulmonary segments?
o: Pulmonary artery is specific for each segment
Each segment is having its own tertiary bronchus
Pulmonary veins are present in between two segments
Most dependent segment is superobasal in standing position
e:
This is an EXCEPT question. Find the false statement about bronchopulmonary segments. In the standing position the most dependent segment is the posterior basal segment of the lower lobe; the superior (apical) segment of the lower lobe is the dependent one in the supine position. So 'superobasal' is incorrect (no such named segment).
| Page : 3
Key points
Segments are the surgical units of the lung and are separated by connective tissue septa. aspiration in the supine position goes to the apical lower lobe segment.
Why not the other options
The remaining statements are true: each segment has its own segmental (tertiary) bronchus; the segmental artery is a branch of the pulmonary artery specific to that segment; pulmonary veins run between segments (intersegmental plane).

q: A new born was brought to the paediatrician by the parents with the complaints of respiratory difficulty. On examination there is not breath sounds on left side of lung. Also, apex beat shifted to right side. Which of the following structures are embryologically not developed?
e:
Newborn with respiratory difficulty, absent breath sounds on the left and apex beat shifted to the right = bowel loops in the left chest pushing the mediastinum to the right. This is left congenital diaphragmatic hernia (Bochdalek), due to failure of the pleuroperitoneal membrane to close the posterolateral pericardioperitoneal canal.
Key points
Diaphragm develops from septum transversum, pleuroperitoneal membranes, oesophageal mesentery and body wall muscles.
CDH causes pulmonary hypoplasia.
treat with stabilisation then surgery.
Why not the other options
Hepatic and pancreatic buds form the liver and pancreas and do not seal the diaphragm. The pericardial membrane is not an embryological diaphragm component.

q: A 12-year-old male patient had come to surgical OPD with swelling in the groin. On examination with deep ring occlusion test, swelling is not present. Which of the following hernia is the given case?
e:
A 12-year-old with groin swelling that disappears when the deep ring is occluded. A swelling controlled by deep ring occlusion enters through the deep ring, so it is an indirect inguinal hernia (patent processus vaginalis, common in young males, lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels).
Key points
Indirect: coverings = internal spermatic fascia, cremasteric, external spermatic fascia. Ring occlusion test and Zieman's test differentiate types clinically.
Why not the other options
A direct hernia bulges through Hesselbach's triangle and still protrudes with the deep ring occluded. Femoral hernia is below and lateral to the pubic tubercle; umbilical hernia is at the umbilicus.
| Page : 4

q: A 69-year-old male patient is diagnosed with Chronic myeloid leukaemia, and on abdominal examination, there is splenomegaly is observed towards the right inguinal region but not to left inguinal region. Which of the following ligaments are responsible for the change in direction of splenomegaly?
e:
CML with massive splenomegaly growing towards the right inguinal/iliac region but not the left. The phrenicocolic ligament (from the splenic flexure to the diaphragm) forms a shelf under the spleen and blocks its descent along the left flank, so the enlarged spleen is directed obliquely downwards and medially towards the right iliac fossa.
Key points
Splenomegaly notch is on the medial border.
massive splenomegaly (CML, kala-azar, myelofibrosis) crosses the midline.
Why not the other options
The gastrosplenic and lienorenal (splenorenal) ligaments carry the short gastric and splenic vessels; the greater omentum is a peritoneal apron and does not direct spleen growth.

q: A 60-year-old person had come to surgical OPD with a mass at the anal verge. On examination it was identified as carcinoma. Which of the following lymph nodes are affected in this case?
e:
Carcinoma at the anal VERGE (below the pectinate/dentate line). Lymph from the anal canal below the pectinate line and perianal skin drains to the superficial inguinal nodes, so these enlarge.
Key points
Above the pectinate line: internal iliac and pararectal nodes.
below: superficial inguinal nodes.
Above is endoderm (visceral nerves, painless)
below is ectoderm (somatic nerves, painful).
Why not the other options
Deep inguinal nodes drain the glans penis/clitoris; internal iliac nodes drain the anal canal ABOVE the pectinate line, the rectum and pelvic viscera; external iliac nodes drain the cervix, bladder and deep inguinal nodes.

q: A 3-day old new born was brought to paediatrician with complaints of having greenish discharge from the umbilicus. Which of the following structures abnormality is seen in this case?
e:
A 3-day-old newborn with GREENISH (bile-stained/faecal) discharge from the umbilicus = communication between the gut and the umbilicus. A persistent vitellointestinal (omphalomesenteric) duct, connecting the midgut to the yolk sac, forms an umbilical fistula that discharges intestinal contents (Meckel's diverticulum remnant).
Key points
Meckel's rule of 2s: 2% population, 2 feet from ileocaecal valve, 2 inches long, 2 types of ectopic tissue (gastric and pancreatic).
Why not the other options
Persistent urachus (allantois) discharges urine. Umbilical arteries and vein carry blood and become ligaments; they do not drain gut contents.

q: An old person had hit and run by a car. He was taken to hospital and on examination there was a pelvic fracture. Also he is unable to pass urine without any perineal swellings. Which of the following urethra got damaged?
e:
Road accident with a pelvic fracture; the man cannot pass urine; there is NO perineal swelling. Pelvic fractures typically shear the membranous urethra (fixed in the urogenital diaphragm, above the perineal membrane). Extravasated urine stays in the extraperitoneal pelvis, so no perineal swelling appears.
Key points
Posterior urethra (prostatic and membranous) = pelvic fracture, high-riding prostate. anterior urethra (bulbar, penile) = straddle injury.
Why not the other options
Bulbar urethra injury (straddle injury) is below the perineal membrane and gives a butterfly-shaped perineal haematoma and swelling. Prostatic urethra is rarely injured; penile urethra is injured by direct trauma.

q: A 45-year-old person on standing on right side foot with left foot off the ground, pelvis sags down to left side. While walking he swayed to right side. Which of the following nerve is damaged?
e:
Standing on the right leg the pelvis sags to the LEFT; while walking he sways to the right = positive Trendelenburg sign/gait on the right side. Gluteus medius and minimus (abductors) hold the pelvis level in single-leg stance. They are supplied by the superior gluteal nerve; when it is damaged the pelvis drops on the opposite (unsupported) side, and the body lurches to the affected side.
Key points
Causes: injury during gluteal intramuscular injection, hip surgery, poliomyelitis, hip dislocation.
Why not the other options
Inferior gluteal nerve supplies gluteus maximus (weak rising from sitting, climbing). Femoral nerve supplies quadriceps (knee extension). Obturator nerve supplies adductors.
| Page : 6

q: A teacher beaten student with the stick and after that the student unable to dorsiflexion and eversion of foot. Which of the following bone got fractured?
e:
A stick beating the leg, then loss of dorsiflexion AND eversion of the foot = foot drop. The common peroneal (fibular) nerve winds around the NECK of the fibula, where it is superficial and fixed, so fracture or direct blow there injures it. Deep peroneal loss gives loss of dorsiflexion; superficial peroneal loss gives loss of eversion.
Key points
Common peroneal nerve is the most commonly injured nerve of the lower limb.
features: foot drop, steppage gait, sensory loss on dorsum of foot.
Why not the other options
Tibial tuberosity (patellar tendon insertion) and fibular shaft are not related to the nerve; the fibular head is closer but the nerve winds distal to it, at the neck.

q: Identify the large cells that shown in the given image
e:
Large cells seen in a cerebellar cortex section. Purkinje cells are the largest neurons of the cerebellar cortex, with flask-shaped cell bodies forming a single row between the molecular and granular layers; their dendrites branch in a plane in the molecular layer.
Key points
Purkinje cells are the only output of the cerebellar cortex (to deep nuclei) and use GABA (inhibitory).
Why not the other options
Granule cells are the smallest and most numerous neurons (granular layer); Golgi cells are larger interneurons in the granular layer but smaller than Purkinje cells; pyramidal cells are found in the cerebral cortex.
| Page : 7

q: A farmer was brought to emergency room after OP poisoning. While inserting tube for the gastric lavage, there was a resistance at 25 cm from the upper incisors. Which of the following structure causes the resistance?
e:
Gastric lavage tube meets resistance at 25 cm from the incisors. The aortic arch indents the oesophagus at about
22.5-25 cm, causing the second constriction.
Key points
Oesophageal constrictions: 15 cm cricopharyngeus, 22.5 cm aortic arch, 27.5 cm left bronchus, 40 cm diaphragm.
Foreign bodies lodge most often at the cricopharyngeus.
Why not the other options
Cricopharyngeus (pharyngo-oesophageal junction) is at 15 cm; left bronchus at 27.5 cm; diaphragm (hiatus) at 40 cm. Only the arch of aorta fits 25 cm.

q: The pressure-volume loop of the left ventricle shifts to the right with an increase in end-diastolic volume, while end-systolic volume remains nearly unchanged. Which physiological change most likely produced this finding?
e:
Increased preload increases left ventricular end-diastolic volume (EDV). By the Frank-Starling mechanism, the greater initial myocardial fiber length produces a stronger contraction and increases stroke volume. If afterload and contractility remain unchanged, end-systolic volume changes little.
Key points
Increased preload → increased EDV → increased stroke volume.
Width of the PV loop = stroke volume.
Increased afterload increases end-systolic volume.
Increased contractility decreases end-systolic volume.

q: During the cardiac cycle, the mitral valve has just closed while the aortic valve remains closed. Which phase of the ventricular cycle is occurring?
e:
When ventricular pressure exceeds atrial pressure, the AV valves close, producing the first heart sound. However, ventricular pressure has not yet exceeded aortic pressure, so the semilunar valves remain closed. Because all valves are closed, ventricular pressure rises rapidly while ventricular volume remains constant.
| Page : 8
Key points
Mitral/tricuspid closure → S1.
Both sets of valves closed → isovolumetric contraction.
Ventricular volume remains at end-diastolic volume during this phase.
Aortic valve opens when LV pressure exceeds aortic pressure.

q: An intravenous fluid infusion increases venous return in a healthy individual without changing myocardial contractility or arterial resistance. Which change is predicted by the Frank-Starling mechanism?
o: Increased end-diastolic volume and increased stroke volume
Increased end-diastolic volume and decreased stroke volume
Decreased end-diastolic volume and increased end-systolic volume
Decreased myocardial fiber length and increased stroke volume
e:
Increased venous return increases ventricular filling and end-diastolic volume. The resulting increase in myocardial fiber length increases the force of contraction, thereby increasing stroke volume. This intrinsic relationship is the Frank-Starling mechanism.
Key points
Increased venous return → increased preload.
Increased preload → increased myocardial fiber length.
Increased fiber length → increased force of contraction and stroke volume.
Frank-Starling regulation does not require increased sympathetic stimulation.

q: A healthy person suddenly stands up from a supine position. The transient decrease in arterial pressure produces which immediate baroreceptor response?
o: Increased carotid sinus firing with increased vagal activity
Decreased carotid sinus firing with increased sympathetic activity
Increased aortic arch firing with decreased sympathetic activity
Decreased carotid sinus firing with decreased heart rate
e:
Standing causes gravitational pooling of blood in the lower extremities, transiently decreasing venous return, cardiac output and arterial pressure. Reduced stretch of the carotid sinus and aortic arch causes decreased baroreceptor firing. This increases sympathetic and decreases parasympathetic outflow, producing tachycardia, increased contractility and peripheral vasoconstriction.
Key points
Decreased BP → decreased baroreceptor stretch and firing.
Increased sympathetic activity → increased HR, contractility and vascular resistance. Carotid sinus afferents travel through CN IX.
Aortic arch afferents travel through CN X.

q: A substance is freely filtered at the glomerulus and is neither reabsorbed nor secreted by the renal tubules. Its urine concentration is 30 mg/mL, urine flow rate is 1 mL/min, and plasma concentration is 0.25 mg/mL. Which parameter is measured by the clearance of this substance?
e:
The substance described is inulin. Because inulin is freely filtered and is neither reabsorbed nor secreted, the amount excreted equals the amount filtered. Therefore, inulin clearance is the reference measurement of GFR. Its clearance is: C = (U × V) / P = (30 × 1) / 0.25 = 120 mL/min Thus, the GFR is 120 mL/min.
Key points
Inulin clearance = GFR.
Inulin is freely filtered.
It is neither reabsorbed nor secreted.
PAH clearance ≈ renal plasma flow.
Creatinine clearance is commonly used clinically to estimate GFR.
Glomerular filtration rate

q: A patient is unable to generate a concentrated urine despite adequate ADH secretion. Dysfunction of which structure would most directly impair maintenance of the renal medullary osmotic gradient?
o: Thick ascending limb of loop of Henle
e:
The thick ascending limb actively reabsorbs Na+, K+, and Cl− through the NKCC2 cotransporter but is essentially impermeable to water. This separates solute from water and is fundamental to the countercurrent multiplier, which establishes the hyperosmotic renal medulla required for concentrating urine.
Key points
Descending limb: highly permeable to water.
Thick ascending limb: reabsorbs Na+-K+-2Cl− and is impermeable to water.
Loop of Henle acts as a countercurrent multiplier.
Vasa recta acts as a countercurrent exchanger.
ADH utilizes the medullary gradient to concentrate urine.

q: As plasma glucose concentration progressively increases, glucose begins to appear in urine before the transport maximum (Tm) for glucose is reached. What best explains this phenomenon?
e:
Splay describes the rounded portion of the glucose titration curve between the renal threshold and the point at which the overall transport maximum is reached. Glucose appears in urine before the theoretical Tm because individual nephrons differ slightly in their transport capacity, and glucose transporters become saturated progressively rather than simultaneously.
Key points
Glucose is freely filtered and normally completely reabsorbed in the proximal tubule. Renal threshold: plasma concentration at which glucose first appears in urine.
Tm: maximal tubular transport capacity.
Splay: gradual saturation of glucose transport among different nephrons.
| Page : 10

q: A patient with diabetic ketoacidosis has the following arterial blood gas values: pH: 7.25 HCO3 : 12 mEq/L PaCO2: 26 mmHg Which acid-base disturbance is present?
o: Metabolic acidosis with appropriate respiratory compensation
Metabolic acidosis with superimposed respiratory acidosis
e:
The low pH indicates acidemia, and the markedly decreased bicarbonate establishes metabolic acidosis as the primary disorder. Using Winter’s formula: Expected PaCO2 = (1.5 × HCO3−) + 8 ± 2 Expected PaCO2 = 26 ± 2 mmHg. The measured PaCO2 is 26 mmHg, indicating appropriate respiratory compensation.
Key points
Metabolic acidosis: decreased HCO3−.
Compensation occurs through hyperventilation and reduction of PaCO2.
Winter’s formula: expected PaCO2 = 1.5 × HCO3− + 8 ± 2.
A measured PaCO2 above the expected range suggests additional respiratory acidosis; below it suggests additional respiratory alkalosis.

q: A pulmonary embolus completely obstructs blood flow to a group of alveoli that continue to receive normal ventilation. What happens to the ventilation-perfusion ratio in these alveoli?
e:
In pulmonary embolism, affected alveoli may remain ventilated while their perfusion approaches zero. Therefore: V/Q → ∞ This represents alveolar dead space.
Key points
V/Q = 0: perfusion without ventilation → shunt.
V/Q → ∞: ventilation without perfusion → dead space.
Pulmonary embolism increases physiological dead space.
Normal whole-lung V/Q is approximately 0.8.

q: A premature neonate develops respiratory distress due to inadequate pulmonary surfactant. Which physiological change is most likely?
o: Increased lung compliance and decreased alveolar surface tension
Decreased lung compliance and increased tendency for alveolar collapse
Increased functional residual capacity due to alveolar overdistension
Decreased elastic recoil of the lungs
e:
Surfactant decreases surface tension at the air-liquid interface of alveoli. Deficiency therefore increases surface tension, making alveoli more likely to collapse and increasing the work required to expand the lungs. Lung compliance consequently decreases.
| Page : 11
Key points
Surfactant is produced by type II pneumocytes.
Major component: dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine (DPPC).
Surfactant decreases surface tension.
It increases lung compliance and helps prevent alveolar collapse.
Deficiency contributes to neonatal respiratory distress syndrome.

q: As blood passes through systemic tissues, CO2 enters red blood cells and is converted to bicarbonate. Which ionic movement across the RBC membrane maintains electrical neutrality during this process?
o: HCO3 enters the RBC while Cl leaves
HCO3 leaves the RBC while Cl enters
H leaves the RBC while Na enters
Cl and HCO3 both leave the RBC
e:
In systemic capillaries, CO2 enters RBCs and is converted by carbonic anhydrase into carbonic acid, which dissociates into H+ and HCO3−. Bicarbonate then moves into plasma in exchange for chloride entering the RBC. This is the chloride shift (Hamburger phenomenon).
Key points
Most CO2 is transported as bicarbonate.
Carbonic anhydrase within RBCs accelerates bicarbonate formation.
In tissues: HCO3− moves out and Cl− moves into RBCs.
The process reverses in pulmonary capillaries.

q: In the pulmonary capillaries, oxygenation of hemoglobin facilitates the unloading of CO2 and H from blood. This phenomenon is known as:
e:
The Haldane effect describes the reduced ability of oxygenated hemoglobin to carry CO2 and H+. Therefore, oxygenation of hemoglobin in the lungs promotes CO2 unloading. In contrast, the Bohr effect describes how increased CO2 and H+ reduce hemoglobin’s affinity for oxygen in peripheral tissues.
Key points
Haldane effect: O2 affects carriage of CO2.
Bohr effect: CO2/H+ affect carriage of O2.
Deoxygenated hemoglobin carries more CO2 and buffers more H+.
The Haldane effect facilitates CO2 elimination in the lungs.

q:
A patient has proximal muscle weakness that improves with repeated muscle activity.
Electrophysiological testing shows increased muscle response with repetitive stimulation. Which abnormality is most likely?
o: Autoantibodies against postsynaptic nicotinic acetylcholine receptors
Autoantibodies against presynaptic voltage-gated Ca² channels
e:
Autoantibodies against presynaptic voltage-gated Ca2+ channels This pattern is characteristic of Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome. Antibodies against presynaptic P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channels reduce calcium entry and therefore decrease acetylcholine release. With repeated stimulation, calcium accumulates in the presynaptic terminal, increasing acetylcholine release and improving muscle strength.
Key points
Lambert-Eaton: presynaptic Ca2+ channels.
Strength often improves with repeated activity.
Myasthenia gravis involves postsynaptic ACh receptors and typically worsens with repeated activity. Lambert-Eaton may be associated with small-cell lung carcinoma.

q: During excessive contraction of a skeletal muscle, increased tension activates a receptor that produces reflex relaxation of the same muscle. Which receptor and afferent fiber mediate this response?
e:
The Golgi tendon organ senses muscle tension. Excessive tension activates group Ib afferent fibers, which stimulate inhibitory interneurons in the spinal cord. These inhibit the alpha motor neurons supplying the same muscle, producing the inverse stretch reflex (autogenic inhibition).
Key points
Muscle spindle: senses muscle length/stretch.
Primary spindle afferent: Ia.
Golgi tendon organ: senses muscle tension.
GTO afferent: Ib.
GTO activation produces autogenic inhibition.

q: A patient has a lesion involving the right cerebellar hemisphere. Which finding is most likely during examination?
o: Right-sided loss of pain and temperature
e:
Cerebellar lesions characteristically produce ipsilateral deficits. A right cerebellar hemisphere lesion therefore causes right-sided limb incoordination, including dysmetria, intention tremor, dysdiadochokinesia, and decomposition of movement. The ipsilateral nature results from the organization and double-crossing of major cerebellar motor pathways.
Key points
Cerebellar signs are generally ipsilateral to the lesion.
Hemisphere lesion → predominantly limb coordination abnormalities.
Intention tremor becomes more prominent as the target is approached.
Vermis lesions predominantly cause truncal and gait ataxia.
Cerebellar lesions cause incoordination rather than paralysis.
| Page : 13

q: Ammonia doesn’t have any function in the body and if it accumulates can be extremely toxic to the brain and cause cerebral edema, it is excreted through ornithine cycle, which is the rate limiting enzyme for this process?
e:
Ammonia is toxic to the brain (cerebral oedema) and is removed by conversion to urea in the urea (ornithine) cycle. The question asks for the RATE-LIMITING enzyme. Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase-1 (CPS-1), in the mitochondrial matrix, forms carbamoyl phosphate from NH3 + CO2 and is the committed step. It is activated allosterically by N-acetylglutamate.
Key points
CPS-1 deficiency and OTC deficiency (X-linked, raised orotic acid) cause hyperammonaemia.
Why not the other options
Argininosuccinate synthase is a later cytosolic enzyme. CPS-2 is cytosolic and belongs to pyrimidine synthesis (inhibited by UTP, activated by PRPP). Fumarate is a product, not an enzyme.

q: Ornithine cycle breaks converts ammonia which is a highly toxic compound into urea which can be excreted to prevent accumulation, this cycle takes place in?
e:
Ammonia is converted to urea before excretion in urine. The urea cycle occurs in the liver (periportal hepatocytes). The first two steps (carbamoyl phosphate and citrulline formation) are mitochondrial; the remaining three steps are cytosolic.
Key points
Glucose-alanine cycle moves muscle ammonia to the liver.
glutamine carries ammonia from brain and other tissues.
Why not the other options
Kidney excretes urea but lacks the complete cycle (it makes arginine from citrulline). Skeletal muscle and bone carry ammonia as alanine and glutamine to the liver.

q: Which of the following is a cofactor of glutathione peroxidase?
e:
The question asks for the cofactor of glutathione peroxidase, an antioxidant enzyme. Glutathione peroxidase is a selenoenzyme containing selenocysteine; it reduces hydrogen peroxide and lipid hydroperoxides using reduced glutathione.
| Page : 14
Key points
Selenium deficiency: Keshan disease (cardiomyopathy)
Selenium toxicity: garlic breath, hair loss.
Why not the other options
Cobalt is part of vitamin B12; molybdenum is a cofactor of xanthine oxidase, sulphite oxidase and aldehyde oxidase; copper is a cofactor of superoxide dismutase (cytosolic), ceruloplasmin and cytochrome oxidase.

q: A 42-year-old man with a history of chronic alcohol use presents with confusion, unsteady gait, and numbness in his feet. On examination, he has impaired coordination and mild ophthalmoplegia. Laboratory evaluation suggests impaired carbohydrate metabolism, and the clinician explains that a vitamin-dependent enzyme in the pentose phosphate pathway is needed for a transketolation reaction. Which of the following vitamin helps in Transketolation?
e:
Chronic alcohol use + confusion + ataxia + ophthalmoplegia + foot numbness = Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome (thiamine deficiency). The enzyme named is TRANSKETOLASE of the pentose phosphate pathway. Thiamine (vitamin B1) as thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP) is the cofactor for transketolase. TPP is also needed by pyruvate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase and branched-chain keto acid dehydrogenase.
Key points
RBC transketolase activity is the test for thiamine status.
Give thiamine BEFORE glucose in alcoholics.
Why not the other options
Riboflavin forms FAD/FMN, niacin forms NAD/NADP, pantothenic acid forms coenzyme A. None acts in transketolation.

q: A 42-year-old man presents with FOLLOWING SYMPTOMS SHOW BELOW IN THE IMAGE and pain in his knees and ankles for the past few weeks. He reports eating mostly processed food and rarely consuming fresh fruits or vegetables. On examination, he has perifollicular hemorrhages and poor wound healing. Which of the following most likely describes this condition?
e:
Processed food, no fruit or vegetables + perifollicular haemorrhages + poor wound healing + joint pain = vitamin C deficiency. Scurvy: vitamin C is required for hydroxylation of proline and lysine in collagen, so collagen is weak, causing perifollicular bleeding, gum bleeding, corkscrew hairs and poor wound healing.
| Page : 15
Key points
Vitamin C also aids iron absorption and is an antioxidant.
scorbutic rosary and subperiosteal haemorrhage in infants.
Why not the other options
Beriberi (B1) has neuropathy or cardiac failure; rickets (vitamin D) causes bone deformities in children; cheilosis (riboflavin or other B vitamins) causes cracks at the mouth angles.

q: One of the following given enzyme is not an oxidoreductase
e:
Pick the enzyme that is NOT an oxidoreductase. Glucokinase (glycokinase) transfers a phosphate group from ATP to glucose, so it is a transferase (class 2), not an oxidoreductase.
Key points
Six enzyme classes: oxidoreductases, transferases, hydrolases, lyases, isomerases, ligases.
Why not the other options
Peroxidase, oxidase and oxygenase all catalyse oxidation-reduction reactions (class 1: dehydrogenases, oxidases, peroxidases, oxygenases, reductases).

q: A 3-year-old boy presents to his physician with photosensitivity, nystagmus, and a failure to thrive. Laboratory tests reveal levels of neutral amino acids in the urine are elevated. The patient is diagnosed with Hartnup disease. Daily supplementation of which of these molecules would alleviate the severity of symptoms of this disorder?
e:
Photosensitivity + cerebellar signs (nystagmus) + failure to thrive + high neutral amino acids in urine = Hartnup disease. Defective neutral amino acid transporter (SLC6A19) in the gut and kidney causes loss of tryptophan, which is the precursor of niacin, so the child develops pellagra-like features. Nicotinic acid supplementation corrects this.
Key points
Pellagra = 3 Ds (dermatitis, diarrhoea, dementia)
tryptophan to niacin needs vitamin B6.
Why not the other options
Tetrahydrobiopterin helps phenylalanine hydroxylase (PKU variants); folic acid is for megaloblastic anaemia; vitamin B6 treats homocystinuria and pyridoxine-responsive disorders.
| Page : 16

q:
The movement of electrons from NADH occurs via complexComplex I: NADH dehydrogenase
Complex II: Succinate dehydrogenase
Complex III: Cytochrome bc1
Complex IV: Cytochrome c oxidase
e:
The question lists complexes I-IV and asks for the path of electrons from NADH. NADH donates electrons to Complex I, then CoQ, then Complex III (cytochrome bc1), cytochrome c and Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase), finally to O2. Sequence = 1-3-4.
Key points
Complex I pumps 4 H+, III pumps 4 H+, IV pumps 2 H+.
Complex II does not pump protons.
Why not the other options
Complex II (succinate dehydrogenase) accepts electrons from FADH2/succinate and feeds CoQ, bypassing Complex I; so any option containing 2 is not the NADH path. 1-4 skips Complex III.

q: A patient with a mitochondrial enzyme defect has impaired conversion of pyruvate into the two-carbon substrate that subsequently enters the TCA cycle. In which cellular compartment does this conversion normally occur?
e:
Pyruvate is being converted into a two-carbon unit that enters the TCA cycle = pyruvate to acetyl-CoA by the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex. PDH complex is located in the mitochondrial matrix, the same site as the TCA cycle.
Key points
PDH cofactors: TPP, lipoic acid, CoA, FAD, NAD (vitamin B1, B2, B3, B5)
PDH deficiency causes lactic acidosis.
Why not the other options
Inner mitochondrial membrane holds the electron transport chain; the cytoplasm is the site of glycolysis (pyruvate formation); ribosomes make proteins.

q: The link reaction is between which two cycles?
e:
The 'link reaction' connects two pathways. The link reaction is the oxidative decarboxylation of pyruvate to acetyl- CoA, joining aerobic glycolysis to the Krebs cycle.
| Page : 17
Key points
PDH reaction is irreversible, so fatty acids cannot be converted back to glucose.
Why not the other options
Anaerobic glycolysis ends in lactate, so it cannot feed acetyl-CoA to the TCA cycle; gluconeogenesis builds glucose and is not linked this way.

q: Which CoA derivative is formed from odd-chain fatty acid oxidation?
e:
The question asks which CoA derivative arises from odd-chain fatty acid oxidation. The last thiolysis step of an odd- chain fatty acid gives acetyl-CoA plus propionyl-CoA (3 carbons).
Key points
Propionyl-CoA to methylmalonyl-CoA (biotin) to succinyl-CoA (B12) enters the TCA cycle. vitamin B12 deficiency raises methylmalonic acid.
Why not the other options
Acetoacetyl-CoA is an intermediate of ketogenesis; malonyl-CoA is the first intermediate of fatty acid synthesis; fumaryl CoA is not a standard metabolite.

q: A 28-year-old woman is brought to the clinic after participating in a prolonged hunger strike for religious reasons. She has not eaten for 5 days, but has been drinking water. She reports weakness and dizziness. On examination, she appears thin and mildly dehydrated, with low muscle mass. Laboratory studies show low serum glucose with elevated ketone levels. Which of the following is the main source of fuel for the body during this period?
e:
She has fasted for 5 days (prolonged starvation), has low glucose, elevated ketones and low muscle mass. After about 3 days of fasting the brain adapts to use ketone bodies as its main fuel, reducing glucose need and sparing muscle protein from gluconeogenesis.
Key points
Red blood cells never use ketones (no mitochondria)
Early fasting uses glycogen, then gluconeogenesis, then ketone bodies.
Why not the other options
Amino acids and glucose support early fasting and gluconeogenesis only; fatty acids are used by muscle and heart but cannot cross the blood-brain barrier; the brain cannot use them directly.
| Page : 18

q: A 28-year-old woman with no known medical illness comes to the clinic for a routine checkup. She reports that she had a large carbohydrate-rich lunch 2 hours ago. Her random blood glucose is mildly elevated, and the liver is actively taking up glucose to store it as glycogen. Which enzyme primarily mediates the postprandial utilization of glucose in the liver?
e:
She ate a carbohydrate-rich meal 2 hours ago; the liver is storing glucose as glycogen after a meal. Glucokinase (hexokinase IV) has a high Km, is not inhibited by glucose-6-phosphate and is induced by insulin, so it works when blood glucose is high (post-prandial).
Key points
Glucokinase is found in liver and pancreatic beta cells (glucose sensor)
Mutations cause MODY 2.
Why not the other options
Hexokinase has a low Km and works in all tissues even at low glucose; fructokinase phosphorylates fructose; PFK-1 is the rate-limiting step of glycolysis, not the first trapping step.

q: Which enzyme is deficient in Niemann-Pick disease?
e:
Niemann-Pick disease: hepatosplenomegaly, foam cells and neurodegeneration, with cherry-red spot in some types. Types A and B are due to sphingomyelinase deficiency, so sphingomyelin accumulates.
Key points
Niemann-Pick: cherry-red spot + hepatosplenomegaly.
Tay-Sachs: cherry-red spot WITHOUT hepatosplenomegaly.
Why not the other options
Hexosaminidase A deficiency causes Tay-Sachs; aryl sulphatase A deficiency causes metachromatic leukodystrophy; alpha-galactosidase A deficiency causes Fabry disease.

q: A 42-year-old woman with a recent febrile illness is evaluated for generalized fatigue. Laboratory testing shows elevated markers of cellular stress, and her physician explains that heat shock proteins help cells maintain protein integrity during stress. Which statement about chaperones is true?
o: HSP 70 family of chaperones bind with hydrophobic amino acid
HSP 60 and 70 are similar in structure
e:
Heat shock proteins (chaperones) protect protein integrity during stress. Choose the true statement. HSP70 binds to exposed hydrophobic amino acid stretches of nascent or unfolded proteins in an ATP-dependent manner, preventing aggregation and helping folding.
| Page : 19
Key points
Heat shock increases HSP expression via HSF1.
HSP60 = chaperonin (GroEL), HSP70 = DnaK in bacteria.
Why not the other options
Chaperones prevent (not cause) misfolding; HSP60 (a barrel-shaped chaperonin) and HSP70 differ structurally; chaperones do help unfold misfolded proteins.

q: A 24-year-old woman is evaluated for recurrent bacterial infections. On examination, she has enlarged tonsils and markedly swollen cervical lymph nodes. Laboratory tests show elevated serum immunoglobulin levels, and a peripheral smear suggests increased plasma cell activity. The attending physician explains that these antibody-producing cells have abundant organelles for making large amounts of secreted protein. Protein synthesis occurs in which of the following site?
e:
Plasma cells (antibody-producing, 'abundant organelles') secrete large amounts of protein. Secretory proteins are synthesised by ribosomes attached to the rough endoplasmic reticulum. Plasma cells have abundant RER.
Key points
Free ribosomes make cytosolic proteins.
RER ribosomes make secretory, membrane and lysosomal proteins.
Why not the other options
Golgi bodies modify, sort and package proteins; mitochondria produce ATP; peroxisomes oxidise very long chain fatty acids and break down H2O2.

q: A researcher studies a cell under heat stress and notices that newly synthesized proteins are not reaching their functional shape. Which process is primarily supported by molecular chaperones to prevent misfolding and maintain normal cellular function? The primary role of chaperones is to help in which of the following processes?
e:
Under heat stress new proteins fail to reach their functional shape; the question asks the primary role of chaperones. Chaperones assist protein FOLDING and prevent misfolding and aggregation.
Key points
Misfolded protein diseases: prion disease, Alzheimer's, cystic fibrosis (delta F508 misfolding).
Why not the other options
They do not synthesise proteins (ribosomes do), degrade them (proteasome/ubiquitin) or denature them.
| Page : 20

q: A 68-year-old man presents with progressive exertional dyspnea, bilateral pedal edema, and fatigue. Echocardiography shows increased ventricular wall thickness with preserved ejection fraction and a restrictive filling pattern. ECG shows low-voltage QRS complexes despite the increased ventricular wall thickness. He also reports a history of bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome. A myocardial biopsy is performed and given belowWhich of the following histopathological findings most likely confirms the underlying diagnosis?
o: Extracellular amorphous eosinophilic deposits showing Congo red positivity with apple-green birefringence
Pale infarcted myocardium staining with triphenyl tetrazolium chloride
Non-caseating granulomas composed of epithelioid cells and multinucleated giant cells
Myocyte disarray with hypertrophied cardiac muscle fibers
e:
The combination of increased ventricular wall thickness + low-voltage QRS + bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome strongly suggests cardiac amyloidosis.
Key points
Amyloid is deposited in the extracellular space of the myocardium.
On H&E, it appears as amorphous, eosinophilic material.
The diagnostic stain is Congo red.
Congo red–positive amyloid shows apple-green birefringence under polarized light.
Cardiac amyloid causes a restrictive cardiomyopathy with preserved ejection fraction initially.
A. Congo red + apple-green birefringence → Amyloidosis
Classic confirmatory finding.
C. Non-caseating granulomas → Sarcoidosis
Granulomas contain epithelioid cells ± giant cells.
D. Myocyte disarray → Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
Hypertrophied cardiac myocytes are arranged haphazardly.
Triphenyl tetrazolium chloride (TTC) → Myocardial infarction
Viable myocardium stains red; infarcted tissue remains pale.
| Page : 21

q:
A 56-year-old man presents with progressive fatigue, recurrent infections, and persistent lower back pain for several months. Laboratory investigations reveal normocytic anemia, hypercalcemia, and a sharp monoclonal spike on serum protein electrophoresis. Skeletal imaging is given below. Which of the following findings is most likely to be seen on peripheral blood smear?
A.
B.
C.
D.
(Choose from the labelled images below.)
e:
The clinical picture is highly suggestive of multiple myeloma:
Key points
Monoclonal spike → monoclonal immunoglobulin production
Anemia → bone marrow infiltration by plasma cells
Hypercalcemia + punched-out lytic lesions → increased bone resorption
Increased circulating immunoglobulins cause RBCs to form stacks of coins, producing rouleaux formation on peripheral smear.

q: A 30-year-old woman presents with painful blisters involving the skin and oral mucosa. Direct immunofluorescence of a perilesional skin biopsy is shown below.Which of the following best describes the underlying mechanism responsible for this condition?
o: IgG antibodies directed against desmoglein 3 causing disruption of intercellular adhesion
IgG antibodies directed against hemidesmosomes causing separation at the dermoepidermal junction
IgE-mediated mast-cell degranulation following exposure to an external allergen
Immune-complex deposition along the basement membrane causing complement-mediated tissue injury
e:
The clinical picture and direct immunofluorescence are characteristic of pemphigus vulgaris.
| Page : 23
Key points
Pemphigus vulgaris is an autoimmune blistering disorder caused by IgG autoantibodies against desmosomal proteins.
The major target is desmoglein 3. Desmoglein 1 may also be involved in more extensive disease. Desmosomes normally maintain adhesion between keratinocytes.
Antibody-mediated disruption of desmosomes → acantholysis → separation of keratinocytes → intraepidermal blister.
Because the split occurs above the basal layer, the characteristic blister is suprabasal. Oral mucosal involvement is common because mucosa predominantly expresses desmoglein 3. Direct immunofluorescence shows intercellular IgG deposition in a “fish-net/chicken-wire” pattern.
A. Anti-desmoglein 3 → Pemphigus vulgaris
- Desmosome → keratinocyte adhesion
- Acantholysis → suprabasal blister
- Fish-net/chicken-wire DIF
B. Anti-hemidesmosomes → Bullous pemphigoid
- Targets BP180 and BP230
- Produces a subepidermal blister
- DIF: linear IgG and C3 along the basement membrane
D. Immune-complex deposition → Type III hypersensitivity
Hypersensitivity
Pemphigus vulgaris = Type II hypersensitivity
The antibodies directly bind to a cell-surface antigen and cause tissue injury by disrupting cell adhesion.A. IgE-mediated mast-cell degranulation → Type I hypersensitivity
Seen in conditions such as anaphylaxis, allergic rhinitis, and urticaria.
Seen in diseases such as SLE, serum sickness, and post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis.
| Page : 24

q: A 12-year-old boy presents with fever, pallor, weight loss, and generalized lymphadenopathy. Peripheral blood examination reveals 80 percent circulating blast cells. Bone marrow examination shows the cells seen in the imageWhich of the following additional findings would most strongly support the diagnosis?
e:
The clinical picture is most consistent with acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), and the age/clinical presentation particularly points toward T-cell ALL.
| Page : 25
Key points
ALL is the most common acute leukemia in children.
Common presentation:
- Fever
- Pallor → anemia
- Weight loss
- Lymphadenopathy
- Bone marrow packed with lymphoblasts
T-cell ALL commonly occurs in older children/adolescent males.
The characteristic associated finding is a mediastinal mass, due to involvement of the thymus.
A. Auer rods → AML
- Needle-shaped azurophilic inclusions in myeloid blasts.
B. t(9;22) → CML
- Philadelphia chromosome.
- BCR-ABL fusion gene.
C. Mediastinal mass → T-cell ALL
- Very high-yield association.
- Think T-cell ALL → thymus → mediastinal mass.
D. Gingival hypertrophy → AML
Especially important in acute promyelocytic leukemia (AML-M3).
Also seen in a subset of ALL, but classically associated with CML.

q: A 65-year-old HIV-positive man presents with fever and progressive breathlessness for 2 weeks. Imaging shows dense infiltration in the lower lobe, and a lung biopsy is performed. The histopathological finding is shown in the imageWhich of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
e:
The biopsy shows enlarged cells with a prominent intranuclear inclusion, producing the classic “owl-eye” appearance, which is characteristic of CMV infection.
| Page : 26
Key points
CMV is an important opportunistic infection in patients with advanced HIV infection.
CMV infects endothelial cells, epithelial cells, and macrophages.
Infected cells become enlarged (cytomegaly).
The characteristic inclusion is a large basophilic intranuclear inclusion surrounded by a clear halo → “owl-eye” inclusion.
CMV can cause pneumonitis, particularly in severely immunocompromised patients.
A. Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia
- Common opportunistic infection in HIV.
- Characteristically causes diffuse interstitial pneumonia.
- Alveoli contain foamy, eosinophilic material.
- Diagnosis can be supported by GMS staining showing cysts.
C. Cryptococcal pneumonia
- Caused by Cryptococcus neoformans.
- Shows encapsulated yeast with narrow-based budding.
- Capsule can be demonstrated by India ink or mucicarmine.
D. Tuberculosis
Characteristically produces caseating granulomas with epithelioid cells and Langhans giant cells. Acid-fast bacilli can be demonstrated using Ziehl-Neelsen stain

q: A woman with a known inherited disorder has three children, all of whom are affected. Her affected daughter later has affected children, whereas her affected son has no affected children. A similar pattern is observed among her affected sisters and their childrenWhich of the following is the most likely mode of inheritance?
e: The pattern is characteristic of mitochondrial inheritance because mitochondrial DNA is transmitted almost exclusively through the mother. An affected mother can transmit the disorder to all her children, regardless of sex. An affected father does not transmit mitochondrial DNA to his children. Therefore, the disorder can pass through affected females across successive generations, while affected males do not transmit it. The pattern is called maternal inheritance. A. X-linked recessive - Mainly affects males. - No father-to-son transmission. - An affected male does not transmit the disorder to all daughters. B. Autosomal recessive - Can affect both sexes. - Usually appears when two carrier parents have an affected child. - Does not show a consistent maternal transmission pattern. C. X-linked dominant - An affected father transmits the disorder to all daughters but no sons. - This is different from the pattern in the question. D. Mitochondrial inheritance - Correct. - Affected mother → can transmit to sons and daughters. - Affected father → no transmission.

q: A 32-year-old man presents with a gradually enlarging, painless testicular mass. On examination, the testis is firm but non-tender. Ultrasound shows a homogeneous, well-defined intratesticular mass. Serum β- hCG is mildly elevated, while serum AFP is normalThe cut surface of the tumor is shown belowWhich of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
e:
Seminoma is the most common pure testicular germ-cell tumor and typically occurs in young to middle-aged adults. The important clues here are:
| Page : 27
Key points
Painless testicular mass → classic presentation of a testicular tumor.
Homogeneous intratesticular mass → typical gross/radiological appearance of seminoma. AFP normal → important clue because seminoma does not produce AFP.
A) Embryonal carcinoma
- Usually occurs in younger adults.
- More aggressive than seminoma.
- Produces a hemorrhagic and necrotic tumor.
B) Seminoma
- Common pure germ-cell tumor in young adult males.
- Microscopy:
- Large cells with clear/pale cytoplasm
- Central nuclei with prominent nucleoli
- Fibrous septa containing lymphocytes
- Classic “fried-egg” appearance
- Usually PLAP positive.
- AFP is normal.
-
β-hCG can be mildly elevated.
- Seminoma is notably radiosensitive.
C) Yolk sac tumor
- Most common testicular germ-cell tumor in children.
- Produces AFP.
- Histology classically shows Schiller-Duval bodies.
D) Choriocarcinoma
- Produces markedly elevated β-hCG.
- Composed of cytotrophoblasts and syncytiotrophoblasts.
- Often presents with early hematogenous spread.
β-hCG may be mildly elevated → due to the presence of syncytiotrophoblastic cells in some seminomas.A) Embryonal carcinoma
May be associated with elevated AFP and/or β-hCG when present as part of a mixed germ-cell tumorB) Seminoma
well-circumscribed, homogeneous, gray-white mass.

q: A 45-year-old woman presents with a slowly enlarging thyroid nodule. Fine-needle aspiration shows clusters of relatively uniform follicular cells. The lesion is subsequently excisedWhich of the following features is most important for distinguishing a follicular carcinoma from a follicular adenoma?
e:
The key distinction between follicular adenoma and follicular carcinoma is invasion. Both tumors can look very similar on cytology because both are composed of follicular cells. Therefore, fine-needle aspiration cannot reliably distinguish follicular adenoma from follicular carcinoma. The diagnosis of follicular carcinoma requires evidence of:
| Page : 28
Key points
Capsular invasion
Vascular invasion
Or both
A) Nuclear grooves
- Classically associated with papillary thyroid carcinoma.
B) Capsular or vascular invasion — Correct
- Adenoma → no invasion
- Carcinoma → capsular and/or vascular invasion
C) Psammoma bodies
- Classically associated with papillary thyroid carcinoma.
- They are concentrically calcified structures.
D) Amyloid deposition
- Characteristic of medullary thyroid carcinoma.
This is why the excised tumor must be examined for invasionA) Nuclear grooves
May also be seen in other thyroid lesions, so they are not the defining feature of follicular carcinomaB) Capsular or vascular invasion — Correct
Vascular invasion is particularly important because it is associated with hematogenous spread. Derived from calcitonin-related peptides produced by tumor cells

q: In a child from Africa presenting with a jaw mass and a translocation of t(8;14), what is the likely diagnosis based on the biopsy findings?
e: Burkitt lymphoma c-myc mutation. EBV+ Genetic mutation: t (8;14), t (8;22), t (2;8) Face/Jaw swelling. LN biopsy: “Starry Sky” appearance

q: A patient with cirrhosis develops a new hepatic mass. Which serum marker is most strongly associated with hepatocellular carcinoma?
e:
Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is strongly associated with elevated AFP, particularly in patients with underlying cirrhosis.
| Page : 29
Key points
AFP is a fetal liver/yolk sac protein that can be re-expressed by malignant hepatocytes. AFP is also associated with yolk sac tumors.
CA-125 → epithelial ovarian carcinoma
CEA → colorectal carcinoma
AFP → HCC, yolk sac tumor
CA 19-9 → pancreatic adenocarcinoma

q: A 10-year-old child has recurrent episodes of painless, non-pitting, non-itchy swelling of the lips (shown below), sometimes with abdominal pain, often after minor trauma. There is no urticaria and the child's father had similar episodes. What is the underlying defect?
e:
Hereditary angioedema = C1 esterase inhibitor (C1-INH) deficiency, autosomal dominant.
Key points
Unchecked kallikrein -> excess bradykinin -> angioedema without urticaria or itching. Lab: low C4 (also during attacks), normal C3.
Laryngeal edema is life-threatening; acute Rx: C1-INH concentrate, icatibant, ecallantide; FFP if unavailable. ACE inhibitors are contraindicated (they also raise bradykinin). CD55/CD59 deficiency causes PNH.

q: A 32-year-old man presents with recurrent painful oral aphthous ulcers for 2 years, a painful scrotal ulcer, tender red nodules over both shins and an episode of red, painful eye with hypopyon. A sterile needle prick on his forearm produces a pustule after 48 hours. What is the most likely diagnosis ?
e:
Behcet disease = variable-vessel vasculitis; strong association with HLA-B51; common along the old Silk Route (Turkey, Middle East).
Key points
Diagnosis: recurrent painful oral ulcers (at least 3/year) plus 2 of: genital ulcers, eye lesions (uveitis, hypopyon), skin lesions (erythema nodosum), positive pathergy test.
Histology: neutrophilic vasculitis; venous and arterial thrombosis and aneurysms may occur. Treatment: colchicine (mucocutaneous), steroids, azathioprine, anti-TNF for eye disease. SLE oral ulcers are usually painless; IgA vasculitis = palpable purpura, arthritis, abdominal pain in children.

q: A 22-year-old woman presents with menorrhagia and easy bruising since adolescence. Investigations show prolonged bleeding time, prolonged aPTT, normal PT, normal platelet count. What is the most likely diagnosis?
e:
vWD is the most common inherited bleeding disorder; mostly autosomal dominant (type 1).
Key points
vWF mediates platelet adhesion (GpIb) -> raised BT; it also stabilises factor VIII -> low F-VIII -> raised aPTT. Presents with mucocutaneous bleeding (epistaxis, menorrhagia, gum bleeding).
Diagnosis: ristocetin cofactor assay (defective aggregation with ristocetin).
Treatment: desmopressin (DDAVP) for type 1; vWF-containing F-VIII concentrate for severe types.

q: A 35-year-old woman receives a unit of fresh frozen plasma during surgery. Three hours after the transfusion she develops acute dyspnea, fever and hypotension. Chest X-ray shows bilateral pulmonary infiltrates; JVP is normal and echocardiography shows normal cardiac function (non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema). What is the most likely diagnosis?
e:
TRALI = acute non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema with hypoxemia and bilateral infiltrates within 6 hours of transfusion.
Key points
Mechanism: donor anti-HLA / anti-HNA (neutrophil) antibodies activate recipient neutrophils in the lung (two-hit model) -> capillary leak.
Most often after plasma-rich products (FFP, platelets), commonly from multiparous female donors. Features: fever, hypotension, normal JVP and cardiac function; diuretics are not helpful. Management: stop the transfusion, oxygen / ventilatory support; most recover in 48-96 h. It is a leading cause of transfusion-related death.
| Page : 31

q: A 70-year-old man with long-standing ischemic heart disease had repeated episodes of orthopnea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea. He dies, and at autopsy the lungs are heavy, firm and red-brown. Which histological finding is most likely in the lungs?
o: Alveolar spaces filled with neutrophils and fibrin
Non-caseating granulomas with multinucleated giant cells
e:
Left heart failure -> raised pulmonary venous pressure -> chronic passive congestion of the lungs.
Key points
Alveolar microhemorrhages -> macrophages phagocytose RBCs -> hemosiderin-laden macrophages = "heart failure cells" (Perls positive).
Grossly: heavy, firm, red-brown lungs = "brown induration", with septal fibrosis.
Acute congestion shows alveolar edema (pink fluid in alveoli).
Neutrophils + fibrin = lobar pneumonia (red hepatization); non-caseating granulomas = sarcoidosis; lipofuscin = wear-and-tear pigment in the heart and liver.

q: A child presents with fever, sore throat, and an adherent grayish-white pharyngeal membrane. Smear examination shows pleomorphic bacilli with characteristic metachromatic granules. Which special stain is useful for demonstrating these granules?
e:
Fever, sore throat, an ADHERENT grey-white pharyngeal membrane and pleomorphic bacilli with metachromatic granules = diphtheria (Corynebacterium diphtheriae). Albert's stain shows the volutin (metachromatic) granules as blue-black against green bacilli (Ponder's stain is similar).
Key points
Culture on Loeffler's serum slope or potassium tellurite agar.
exotoxin ADP-ribosylates EF-2 (needs the beta-phage)
treat with antitoxin plus penicillin/erythromycin.
Why not the other options
Gram stain only shows Gram-positive rods; Giemsa stains blood parasites and Chlamydia/Rickettsia; India ink shows capsules (Cryptococcus).
| Page : 32

q: Several people develop vomiting within a few hours after eating fried rice and a contaminated sauce at a restaurant. There is no significant fever or inflammatory diarrhea. Which organism is most likely responsible?
e:
Vomiting within a few hours of eating fried rice and a sauce at a restaurant; no fever or inflammatory diarrhoea = pre- formed toxin (food poisoning, not infection). Bacillus cereus emetic type: spores survive cooking, germinate in reheated rice and produce heat-stable cereulide toxin; onset 1-6 hours.
Key points
B. cereus: rice = emetic type.
meat/vegetables = diarrhoeal type (heat-labile enterotoxin).
Why not the other options
Clostridium perfringens gives diarrhoea at 8-16 hours (meat dishes); S. aureus also causes early vomiting but is linked to custard, cream and dairy; C. botulinum causes neuroparalysis, not vomiting.

q: A newborn develops fever, lethargy, seizures, and meningitis shortly after birth. CSF examination shows small Gram-positive rods, and the mother reports consuming unpasteurized dairy products during pregnancy. Which organism is most likely responsible?
e:
Newborn with fever, lethargy, seizures and meningitis + small Gram-positive rods in CSF + mother ate unpasteurised dairy. Listeria monocytogenes is a Gram-positive rod transmitted through unpasteurised milk and soft cheese; it crosses the placenta and causes early-onset neonatal sepsis and meningitis.
Key points
Listeria: tumbling motility, grows at 4 degrees C, beta-haemolytic.
treat with ampicillin plus gentamicin (cephalosporins are NOT active).
Why not the other options
Group B Streptococcus is a Gram-positive COCCUS; Bacillus anthracis is a large Gram-positive spore-forming rod (anthrax); Clostridium tetani causes tetanus (spasms), not meningitis.

q: A 23-year-old woman presents with fever, severe headache, neck stiffness, and a petechial rash. CSF is turbid with neutrophilic pleocytosis, elevated protein, and low glucose. Which organism is most likely responsible?
e:
Fever, severe headache, neck stiffness + PETECHIAL rash + turbid CSF with neutrophils, high protein and low glucose = acute bacterial meningitis with meningococcaemia. Neisseria meningitidis (Gram-negative diplococci) causes meningitis with a petechial/purpuric rash due to endotoxin and DIC.
Key points
Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome.
treat with ceftriaxone.
give rifampicin or ciprofloxacin to close contacts.
vaccine covers A, C, W, Y.
Why not the other options
Pneumococcus causes meningitis but rarely with a petechial rash; Pseudomonas and Francisella do not cause this picture.

q: A patient undergoing endoscopy for chronic dyspepsia has a gastric biopsy tested for urease activity. The organism isolated from the biopsy grows under microaerophilic conditions on selective Skirrow's medium. Which organism is most likely?
e:
Gastric biopsy tested for UREASE activity; grows under MICROAEROPHILIC conditions on Skirrow's medium; chronic dyspepsia. Helicobacter pylori is a urease-positive, microaerophilic curved Gram-negative rod causing gastritis and peptic ulcer.
Key points
Tests: rapid urease test, urea breath test, stool antigen.
treatment is triple therapy (PPI + clarithromycin + amoxicillin).
Why not the other options
Campylobacter jejuni also grows on Skirrow's microaerophilically but is urease-negative (causes diarrhoea); Proteus mirabilis is urease-positive but is a swarming aerobe; E. coli is not microaerophilic or urease-positive.

q: A chronic alcoholic man presents with severe pneumonia. Sputum culture on MacConkey agar produces large, mucoid colonies that ferment lactose. Which organism is most likely responsible?
e:
Chronic alcoholic with severe pneumonia; sputum on MacConkey agar shows LARGE MUCOID colonies that ferment lactose. Klebsiella pneumoniae is a capsulated lactose fermenter (mucoid colonies); it causes lobar pneumonia with 'currant jelly' sputum in alcoholics and diabetics.
Key points
Klebsiella is non-motile.
it causes upper lobe cavitation and bulging fissure sign.
Why not the other options
E. coli ferments lactose but is non-mucoid and not a typical pneumonia pathogen; Moraxella catarrhalis does not ferment lactose; Burkholderia pseudomallei is a non-lactose fermenter.
| Page : 34

q: A hospitalized patient develops a catheter-associated urinary tract infection after several weeks of admission. Urine culture on blood agar shows characteristic concentric waves of spreading growth across the plate. Which organism is most likely responsible?
e:
Catheter-associated UTI after weeks in hospital; growth spreads in CONCENTRIC WAVES on blood agar = swarming motility. Proteus species show swarming growth on blood agar; they also produce urease (alkaline urine, struvite stones).
Key points
Swarming can be prevented by adding chloral hydrate or using MacConkey agar.
Proteus OX-19 and OX-K are used in the Weil-Felix test.
Why not the other options
Pseudomonas gives a blue-green pigment and fruity odour; E. coli and Klebsiella do not swarm.

q: A child with sickle cell anemia presents with recurrent bone pain and fever. Imaging shows multiple areas of non-suppurative osteomyelitis. Which organism is particularly associated with osteomyelitis in patients with sickle cell disease?
e:
Sickle cell child with recurrent bone pain and fever; imaging shows multifocal NON-suppurative osteomyelitis. Salmonella species (typically non-typhoidal) cause osteomyelitis in sickle cell disease because of functional asplenia and bone infarcts that provide a nidus.
Key points
Sickle cell: encapsulated organism infections (pneumococcus) plus Salmonella osteomyelitis.
Why not the other options
Staphylococcus aureus is the commonest cause of osteomyelitis overall; Haemophilus influenzae and Enterobacter are not specifically associated with sickle cell bone disease.
| Page : 35

q: An unvaccinated child presents with high-grade fever, cough, coryza, and conjunctivitis. Bluish-white spots are seen on the buccal mucosa, followed by a maculopapular rash that begins behind the ears and spreads downward. What is the most likely diagnosis?
e:
Unvaccinated child + high fever, cough, coryza and conjunctivitis (3 Cs) + bluish-white buccal spots (Koplik spots) + rash starting behind the ears and spreading downwards. This is measles (paramyxovirus). Koplik spots are pathognomonic and the rash spreads cephalocaudally.
Key points
Complications: pneumonia, otitis media, SSPE (late)
Vitamin A is given to all children with measles.
Why not the other options
German measles (rubella) is milder with posterior auricular nodes and no Koplik spots; roseola infantum gives rash AFTER the fever subsides; scarlet fever has a sandpaper rash with strawberry tongue.

q: A young child presents with severe watery diarrhea and dehydration. Electron microscopy of the stool is shown. Which of the following best describes the causative virus?
o: A dsRNA virus with 11 segmented genome pieces belonging to the Reoviridae family
An enveloped +ssRNA virus transmitted primarily by respiratory droplets
A non-enveloped DNA virus causing slapped-cheek rash in children
A retrovirus with a diploid RNA genome that integrates into host DNA
e:
Young child with severe watery diarrhoea and dehydration; EM shows a wheel-shaped virus. Rotavirus is a non- enveloped dsRNA virus with 11 segments (Reoviridae) and the commonest cause of severe diarrhoea in children.
Key points
Treat with ORS and zinc.
rotavirus vaccine is part of India's UIP.
segmentation allows reassortment.
Why not the other options
Enveloped +ssRNA respiratory virus = coronavirus; non-enveloped DNA virus with slapped-cheek rash = parvovirus B19; retrovirus with integrating diploid RNA = HIV.
| Page : 36

q: A patient with severe immunosuppression develops pneumonia and systemic symptoms. Histological examination shows both intranuclear and intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies within enlarged cells. Which virus is most likely responsible?
e:
Severely immunosuppressed patient with pneumonia + enlarged cells with BOTH intranuclear and intracytoplasmic inclusions. Cytomegalovirus produces cytomegalic cells with an intranuclear 'owl's eye' inclusion and smaller cytoplasmic inclusions.
Key points
CMV causes retinitis, colitis and pneumonitis in AIDS and transplant patients.
treat with ganciclovir.
Why not the other options
Poxvirus has cytoplasmic (Guarnieri) inclusions only; HSV has intranuclear inclusions (Cowdry A) only; mumps virus has cytoplasmic inclusions.

q: A medical student is reviewing viral genome organization. Which of the following viruses has a non- segmented genome?
e:
Find the virus with a NON-SEGMENTED genome. Coronavirus has a single, non-segmented +ssRNA genome.
Key points
Segmented genomes allow reassortment and antigenic shift (influenza)
Mnemonic: BOAR = Bunya, Orthomyxo, Arena, Reo.
Why not the other options
Influenza (8 segments), Bunyavirus (3), Arenavirus (2) have segmented genomes, as does rotavirus (11).

q: A blood product is treated with a solvent-detergent method that disrupts viral envelopes. Which hepatitis virus can still remain infectious because it lacks a lipid envelope?
e:
Solvent-detergent treatment disrupts viral ENVELOPES; which hepatitis virus can survive because it lacks a lipid envelope? Hepatitis A virus is a non-enveloped (naked) picornavirus and is resistant to solvents, detergents and bile.
Key points
HAV (and HEV) are non-enveloped, faeco-orally spread viruses.
plasma derivatives can still transmit them.
| Page : 37
Why not the other options
HIV, hepatitis B and hepatitis C viruses are enveloped and are inactivated by the solvent-detergent method.

q: A 32-year-old woman presents for routine cervical cancer screening. Her HPV test is positive for a high- risk genotype associated with cervical carcinoma. Which HPV types are most strongly associated with cervical cancer?
e:
Positive high-risk HPV test; which types are linked to cervical carcinoma? HPV 16 and 18 cause about 70% of cervical cancers (E6 inactivates p53; E7 inactivates Rb).
Key points
Vaccines (bivalent, quadrivalent, 9-valent) prevent cervical cancer.
Pap smear and HPV DNA test screen for it.
Why not the other options
HPV 6 and 11 cause genital warts (low risk); HPV 1 and 2 cause common/plantar warts; 31 and 32 are not the leading oncogenic types (31 is high risk but less common; 32 is oral).

q: A patient had dengue fever caused by one serotype two years ago and now develops dengue infection with a different serotype. Compared with a primary infection, which complication is the patient at increased risk for?
o: No risk of dengue hemorrhagic fever
Previous infection has no effect on disease severity
Dengue hemorrhagic fever due to antibody-dependent enhancement
The second infection will always be milder
e:
A prior dengue infection with one serotype and now a DIFFERENT serotype (secondary heterotypic infection). Pre- existing non-neutralising antibodies bind the new serotype and increase its uptake into macrophages (antibody- dependent enhancement), causing dengue haemorrhagic fever or shock syndrome.
Key points
Warning signs: abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, bleeding, rising haematocrit with falling platelets. Primary infection gives life-long immunity only to that serotype.
Why not the other options
Statements saying there is no risk, no effect, or a milder second infection are incorrect.
| Page : 38

q: A 42-year-old farmer is brought to the emergency department after he was found unwell while spraying an insecticide in his agricultural field. His clothes and skin had been heavily contaminated with the chemical. Shortly after exposure, he developed profuse sweating, excessive salivation, lacrimation, abdominal cramps, repeated vomiting, and diarrhea. On examination, he is restless and dyspneic. His pupils are markedly constricted. His pulse is 48/min, blood pressure is low, and chest examination reveals diffuse wheeze with copious bronchial secretions. He has involuntary urination, and progressive skeletal muscle weakness. Which of the following statement is not correct regarding this clinical scenario?
o: Carbamates are reversible inhibitors of acetylcholinesterase.
Atropine can be used in both organophosphate and carbamate poisoning
Pralidoxime has a very good therapeutic effect in carbamate poisoning.
Atropine cannot treat the skeletal muscle weakness seen in this patient.
e:
Pralidoxime (2-PAM) is useful for organophosphate poisoning, where it can reactivate phosphorylated AChE before significant aging occurs.Goodman & Gilman specifically states that oximes are not effective against the more rapidly hydrolyzing carbamoyl ester inhibitors and that 2-PAM is not recommended for poisoning with carbamoylating insecticides such as carbaryl.
Key points
Muscarinic manifestations: miosis, bronchoconstriction, increased bronchial/salivary secretions, vomiting/diarrhea, involuntary urination, lacrimation, and bradycardia.
Nicotinic manifestations: fasciculations → fatigability → generalized weakness → severe paralysis; respiratory muscle paralysis is particularly dangerous.
Atropine → treats muscarinic manifestations, especially bronchial secretions, bronchoconstriction, and bradycardia. It does not treat skeletal muscle weakness.
Organophosphate poisoning → atropine + an AChE reactivating oxime such as pralidoxime. Early pralidoxime is important because phosphorylated AChE may undergo aging, after which reactivation becomes ineffective.

q: A 62-year-old man presents with gradually progressive loss of peripheral vision. Ophthalmic examination shows increased intraocular pressure with characteristic optic disc cupping, and gonioscopy reveals an open anterior chamber angle. He also has a long-standing history of bronchial asthma. The ophthalmologist is considering adding a topical drug while minimizing the risk of worsening his respiratory disease. Which beta blocker can be used in this condition?
e:
Betaxolol is a β1-selective blocker used for glaucoma. It has a lower incidence of respiratory adverse effects than timolol, making it the preferred β-blocker among these options in a patient with asthma. It is still used cautiously in asthma.
Key points
Open-angle glaucoma → prostaglandin analogues are preferred first-line medical therapy. Latanoprost Asthma + glaucoma requiring a β-blocker → Betaxolol because it is β1-selective and causes fewer respiratory problems than timolol.
Timolol → nonselective β-blocker → can exacerbate asthma/COPD.
Acute angle-closure glaucoma → first reduce markedly elevated IOP by I.V Mannitol ; pilocarpine is then used as a miotic.
| Page : 39

q: A 34-year-old man presents with marked polyuria and polydipsia, passing nearly 7–8 L of very dilute urine per day. His plasma osmolality is high-normal, while urine osmolality remains very low. After administration of desmopressin, there is little to no increase in urine osmolality, suggesting that the kidneys are unable to respond appropriately to the antidiuretic hormone. What is the mechanism of action of the drug that can be used in this condition?
o: It acts predominantly on the proximal convoluted tubule, causing increased sodium and water loss.
It acts on the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle, causing increased sodium and water loss.
It acts on the distal convoluted tubule, causing mild sodium and water loss, which produces volume contraction and thereby increases proximal tubular sodium and water reabsorption.
It blocks the ENaC channel in the cortical collecting duct, thereby decreasing sodium reabsorption.
e:
It acts on the distal convoluted tubule, causing mild sodium and water loss, which produces volume contraction and thereby increases proximal tubular sodium and water reabsorption. Thiazides inhibit Na+-Cl+ transport in the DCT. The resulting mild volume contraction increases proximal tubular water reabsorption, reducing distal delivery and paradoxically decreasing urine volume.
Key points
Polyuria + polydipsia + dilute urine + failure to respond to desmopressin → nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. Thiazides are a mainstay of treatment for nephrogenic DI
Thiazides additionally block the ability of the DCT to form dilute urine, thereby increasing urine osmolality. Loop diuretics → thick ascending limb → inhibit Na+-K+-2Cl− symporter.
Amiloride → ENaC blocker → especially useful in lithium-induced nephrogenic DI.

q: A 22-year-old medical student has recurrent sneezing, watery rhinorrhea, nasal itching, and watering of the eyes, especially after exposure to dust. She has been taking cetirizine, which controls her symptoms well, but she complains of daytime drowsiness that interferes with her lectures and study sessions. She wants an antihistamine that will control her allergic symptoms with minimal risk of sedation. What would be the best treatment option for this patient?
e:
A second-generation H1 antihistamine used for allergic rhinitis. It penetrates the CNS poorly and Goodman & Gilman describes it as least sedating.
Key points
Cetirizine is a second-generation H1 antihistamine, but it has a somewhat higher incidence of drowsiness than most other second-generation agents.
Fexofenadine → non-sedating second-generation H1 antihistamine and is used for allergic rhinitis. First-generation H1 blockers commonly cause sedation because they enter the CNS more readily. Doxylamine + pyridoxine (vitamin B6) → used for morning sickness .
Olopatadine → vernal keratoconjunctivitis
Astemizole and terfenadine → QT prolongation
| Page : 40

q: A 58-year-old man with a chronic inflammatory joint disorder presents with worsening pain, morning stiffness, and swelling of multiple joints. He has a past history of peptic ulcer disease with an episode of upper gastrointestinal bleeding. The physician wants to prescribe an NSAID for symptomatic relief but prefers an agent with lower risk of gastric mucosal injury. Which of the following drugs is the most appropriate choice in this patient?
e:
Etoricoxib is a selective COX-2 inhibitor. Selective COX-2 inhibitors were developed to maintain anti-inflammatory efficacy while providing better gastrointestinal tolerability than nonselective NSAIDs.
Key points
COX-1 inhibition → gastric mucosal injury + GI bleeding.
Selective COX-2 inhibitors → less GI toxicity than traditional nonselective NSAIDs.
Etoricoxib → highly selective COX-2 inhibitor . COX-2 selectivity improves GI tolerability but may increase cardiovascular thrombotic risk, including myocardial infarction and stroke.
Ibuprofen → used for pharmacological closure of patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) in premature infants. Alprostadil (PGE1) → keeps the ductus arteriosus patent in neonates with certain congenital heart diseases until definitive surgery can be performed.
Misoprostol (PGE1 analogue) + mifepristone → used for termination of early pregnancy.

q: A 46-year-old man presents with a productive cough with thick, tenacious sputum that is difficult to expectorate. The physician prescribes N-acetylcysteine . Which of the following best describes the mechanism of action of this drug?
o: Breaks disulfide bonds in mucus glycoproteins
e:
N-acetylcysteine reduces mucus viscosity by breaking disulfide bonds in mucoproteins/mucus glycoproteins, making sputum easier to clear.
Key points
N-acetylcysteine → mucolytic → breaks disulfide bonds → ↓ mucus viscosity.
N-acetylcysteine is also the antidote for paracetamol toxicity because it replenishes glutathione stores. Ambroxol/Bromhexine → depolymerization of mucopolysaccharides + improved mucociliary clearance.
